impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. The case has major implications for the scope of written-description and enablement requirements for antibody and biologic patents, particularly genus claims in the pharmaceutical space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of pharmaceutical and biotech companies to enforce broad antibody patent claims, protecting significant R&D investments in biologics and providing stronger exclusivity positions for blockbuster drug classes like CGRP-targeting migraine treatments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates greater risk for generic and biosimilar companies seeking to enter markets covered by genus-level biologic patents, potentially extending periods of market exclusivity and delaying competition.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and a model of function calls are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in awarding damages based on foreign sales of infringing software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $185 million infringement judgment, holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and require further proceedings on step two. The court also held that damages based on foreign sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing territorial limits on patent damages. Enhanced damages and attorneys' fees were also vacated due to an improper contempt finding against defendant's counsel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Benefits technology companies facing patent assertions by strengthening Alice § 101 defenses for software patents and clarifying that patent damages generally cannot reach foreign sales, limiting potential exposure in cross-border software infringement cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders asserting software-implemented inventions face heightened invalidity risk under § 101 and reduced damages potential for globally distributed software products.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality principles where the accused multicore processor selection method was largely performed abroad, and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed the territorial reach of U.S. patent law in the context of multicore processor technology, partially reversing and partially affirming summary judgment of noninfringement. The decision clarifies the application of extraterritoriality principles to method claims where steps occur both domestically and abroad, with significant implications for semiconductor and technology companies operating global supply chains.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with clearer guidance on extraterritoriality defenses against patent infringement claims when manufacturing and design processes span multiple jurisdictions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting method claims against products manufactured through global processes may find it more difficult to establish infringement occurring within the United States.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that asked a single infringement question covering all asserted patents, without identifying which patent(s) were infringed, requires vacatur of the infringement and damages judgments, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis of the '495 patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding that a verdict form combining infringement questions for multiple patents into a single question was prejudicially erroneous. The court also vacated and remanded the § 101 eligibility determination for the '495 patent under Alice step two, while affirming eligibility for other asserted patents related to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers stronger grounds to challenge ambiguous verdict forms in multi-patent cases, potentially reducing exposure to overbroad damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders must ensure verdict forms separately address each asserted patent, increasing trial complexity and the risk that favorable verdicts may be vacated on procedural grounds.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiffs presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that each asserted trade secret was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether inventorship claims based on the same allegedly secret ideas survive when the ideas are found to be generally known.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed trade secret misappropriation and breach-of-contract verdicts, holding there was insufficient evidence that the claimed information constituted protectable trade secrets under California law. The court also reversed a patent inventorship correction, finding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting verdict was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clearer standards for defendants challenging trade secret claims, reinforcing that plaintiffs must demonstrate information is not generally known in the relevant industry to qualify for trade secret protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must more rigorously document the secrecy and novelty of their claimed information, as courts will scrutinize whether asserted trade secrets were actually generally known.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Defend Trade Secrets Act's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet brought its trade secret misappropriation claim, given that Insulet allegedly knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA, holding that the statute of limitations had expired because Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. This is a significant ruling on the DTSA's limitations period and when the discovery rule triggers the clock.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a stronger limitations defense, particularly where the plaintiff had early indicators of potential misappropriation but delayed filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly once they become aware of potential misappropriation or risk losing the ability to pursue DTSA claims, even if they delay to investigate the full scope of the wrongdoing.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims related to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications (e.g., television broadcasting), while affirming eligibility for others. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, sustaining a willful infringement finding against LG. The decision provides important guidance on § 101 eligibility for claims at the boundary of mathematical algorithms and concrete technological improvements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology gain clarity that claims tied to concrete technical improvements in signal processing may survive § 101 challenges, supporting enforcement of standards-essential and related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement risk and must carefully evaluate the eligibility of asserted claims before assuming § 101 provides a defense.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data through passive data collection devices are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case qualifies as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that claims directed to automated farming data collection and sharing systems are patent-ineligible under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285. The ruling reinforces that claims reciting conventional data collection and processing steps applied to agriculture may be abstract, while signaling that asserting such weak patents may warrant fee-shifting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies and other defendants facing data-collection patent assertions gain stronger § 101 defenses, and the remand on exceptionality may deter weak patent enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the agricultural technology and IoT data-collection space face heightened risk that their claims will be found abstract, and may face attorneys' fee awards for pursuing enforcement.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify at summary judgment about matters outside their personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose a device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify on matters beyond their personal knowledge and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's functionality in the sale itself. The ruling has significant implications for how prior art sales evidence is marshaled and the scope of the on-sale bar defense.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity gain broader evidentiary tools, as 30(b)(6) testimony on historical sales is admissible even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, strengthening on-sale bar defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from historical commercial sales of predecessor products, even where the sales did not publicly disclose the relevant functionality.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license to a third party. The decision clarifies standing requirements for patent owners who structure licensing agreements to retain enforcement rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure licensing agreements to retain litigation rights while monetizing patents through exclusive licenses, preserving their ability to enforce patents against infringers without joining the licensee.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a standing-based defense when the patent owner retains an explicit right to sue, even if most commercial rights have been exclusively licensed to a third party.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it had previously filed a declaratory judgment action and missed the deadline for seeking a stay under the statute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of a district court action by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. This prevents gamesmanship in the coordination between ITC investigations and parallel district court patent litigation, particularly in the pharmaceutical context where timing is critical.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners pursuing ITC investigations benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate statutory stay provisions through strategic refiling, preserving parallel district court proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents must be diligent in seeking mandatory stays within statutory deadlines and cannot reset the clock by refiling declaratory judgment actions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents for wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's limited exclusion order barring importation of Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement technology found to infringe Masimo's patents. The court upheld the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings. This high-profile decision impacts Apple's ability to sell watches with the blood oxygen feature in the United States.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders, particularly medical device companies, gain confidence that the ITC remains a powerful venue for enforcing patents against large technology companies importing infringing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies incorporating health-monitoring features into consumer electronics face significant import exclusion risk and must conduct thorough freedom-to-operate analyses before product launches.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination of claims directed to sensor-based logistics systems, specifically regarding dependent claims requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination in an IPR where Qualcomm challenged FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding that the Board's analysis was insufficient as to certain dependent claims. The case also raised issues about third-party IPR petitioners filing on the filing deadline of the party actually sued for infringement, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of termination.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of PTAB obviousness findings, particularly for dependent claims with specific technical limitations that distinguish over the prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Third-party IPR petitioners may face increased scrutiny regarding their relationship to defendants in parallel litigation, though the court did not resolve the real-party-in-interest issue here.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in approving a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER fees, and whether incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives are permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary improperly used PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld attorneys' fee awards and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges to jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and the propriety of service awards. The decision validates the use of incentive awards for organizational class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates incentive awards for class representatives and provides a framework for settling government overcharge class actions, giving businesses confidence in the finality of large-scale class settlements.

impacts.caseName: Fuente Marketing Ltd. v. Vaporous Technologies, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there is a likelihood of confusion between a registered standard character 'X' trademark for cigars and an applied-for mark consisting of a stylized 'X' with a dot above it for oral vaporizers.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the TTAB's dismissal of a trademark opposition, finding no likelihood of confusion between Fuente's standard character 'X' mark for cigars and Vaporous's stylized 'X dot' mark for oral vaporizers. Despite overlapping trade channels in smoking-related products, the dissimilarity of the marks outweighed other DuPont factors. The decision provides guidance on how single-letter marks are evaluated for likelihood of confusion.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies adopting stylized marks incorporating common letters gain comfort that visual distinctiveness can overcome likelihood-of-confusion challenges even in related product categories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Owners of single-letter standard character marks may find it difficult to block registration of stylized marks incorporating the same letter, limiting the scope of protection for simple marks.
